lesson.title: How work grows: big O

chapters.label: Fast in class, slow at scale

scenes.narration: A student’s program checked our class of thirty for shared birthdays in a blink. Then he ran it on the whole university, a million students. It would have taken about fourteen hours.
Today: how work grows as the input grows, and big O.

Seconds depend on the phone, so count steps instead. To find the top mark, this loop looks at every mark once. Four marks, four looks; a thousand marks, a thousand looks. The work grows in step with n, the number of items: we write O of n.

Some work grows far more slowly. Binary search halves a sorted list at every look. A thousand names take about ten looks, and a million only about twenty. Doubling the list adds just one look: that’s O of log n.

Now two loops, one inside the other. For each item, the inner loop compares it with every item after it. Three items make three pairs, but a thousand make about half a million. The work grows with the square of the size: O of n squared.

Big O names how the work grows, ignoring small details. O of one: the same work however big, like reading the first item. Log n: halving. N: one pass. N log n: a good sort, like merge sort. N squared: every pair.
Quick check! A program compares every pair of students for a shared birthday. The class doubles in size. About how much more work does it do?
About four times: twice the students, each compared with twice as many others. On a phone that does ten million steps a second, a thousand students take a blink. A million take about fourteen hours.

scenes.on_screen_text: From n² to n: a set
scenes.narration: So fix the method, not the phone. Instead of comparing every pair, remember what you’ve seen in a set. Checking a set takes about the same time however big it grows. One pass is enough: O of n instead of n squared.
Watch for hidden loops. Checking x in a list looks at the items one by one, so inside another loop it makes n squared. Sorting is n log n. A set or a dictionary finds a key in about one step.

In the app, open How work grows. Grow the class from ten to a thousand pupils, and watch all four jobs, from finding a name to checking every pair. Then read the million row, and see which jobs a phone could still finish.
Your turn. A duplicate check compares every pair, and it’s too slow for a million records. Which change helps most?

Remember what you’ve seen in a set. In short: count steps, not seconds. Big O says how work grows: one, log n, n, n log n, n squared. Doubling n quadruples n squared. And a better method beats a faster phone.

scenes.on_screen_text: Try it on your own code
scenes.narration: Try it on your own code: take a program you wrote this term. Find every loop, and every loop hiding inside a line. If two are nested over the same data, replace one with a set or a dictionary.

checkpoints.prompt: Every pair of students is compared. The class doubles. About how much more work?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — every-pair work is O(n²): twice the students, each compared with twice as many, makes four times the work.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with every pair, each of twice as many students meets twice as many others: about four times the work.

checkpoints.prompt: A duplicate check compares every pair and is too slow for a million records. What helps most?

options.text: Remember seen values in a set
Run it on a faster phone

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a set makes it one pass, O(n): well under a second instead of hours.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a faster phone saves a little; a set changes O(n²) to O(n), from hours to well under a second.
